content: Carnitine is a quaternary amino acid that plays a critical role in the oxidation of long-chain fatty acids. Both breast milk and infant formulas naturally contain carnitine. However, parenteral nutrition solutions, which are used to provide nutrients intravenously, do not routinely include carnitine. Neonates who are fed exclusively through parenteral nutrition without carnitine supplementation exhibit significantly reduced tissue carnitine levels. The clinical implications of this deficiency remain uncertain. It has been hypothesized that carnitine deficiency may contribute to the limited ability of premature infants to metabolize lipids provided through parenteral nutrition. Laboratory studies have demonstrated that fatty acid oxidation becomes impaired when tissue carnitine levels drop below 10% of normal, potentially leading to reduced energy availability and impaired growth in these infants. The primary objective of this review was to evaluate whether carnitine supplementation in neonates receiving parenteral nutrition improves weight gain. Secondary objectives included assessing the effects of supplementation on lipid tolerance and ketogenesis. To address these questions, comprehensive searches of multiple databases, including Medline, Embase, The National Research Register (UK), and the Cochrane Controlled Trials Register, were conducted. The search strategy utilized the MeSH terms carnitine and parenteral nutrition. Only randomized controlled trials were included in the review. Eligible studies were required to involve neonates receiving parenteral nutrition with carnitine supplementation as the sole intervention and to measure at least one relevant outcome, such as weight gain, plasma fatty acid levels, plasma triglycerides, lipid tolerance, respiratory quotient, or beta-hydroxybutyrate levels. Two independent reviewers conducted the literature search and reached a consensus on the inclusion of studies. Data extraction and evaluation were performed independently by both reviewers. When necessary, study authors were contacted to clarify or provide missing data. A total of 14 studies were identified, of which six met the inclusion criteria. The included studies varied in their design and outcomes, and most were of short duration. One study assessed both short-term and long-term weight gain, three studies focused solely on short-term weight gain, three studies reported biochemical responses to a short lipid challenge, and two studies evaluated outcomes during routine parenteral nutrition. The findings of the review revealed no evidence that carnitine supplementation in parenterally fed neonates had any significant effect on weight gain, lipid utilization, or ketogenesis. The authors concluded that there is no justification for the routine supplementation of carnitine in neonates receiving parenteral nutrition.
